name: dudo-core
description: Dudo-Core — deployment tooling for the Cloudflare Worker. See wrangler.jsonc.
//workspaces: Added 2026-09-09 per docs/decisions/0040. ONLY THE TWO PACKAGES THAT EXIST TODAY ARE LISTED. `packages/ui` and `packages/client-kdf` join as they are created, in the change that creates them — a workspace entry pointing at a directory that does not exist is a config that fails on install for a reason unrelated to whatever the installer was doing. ORDER MATTERED AND WAS INVERTED FROM 0040's FIRST DRAFT: `platform/admin` was pinned to exact versions BEFORE this key landed, because hoisting a caret range makes a package's resolution a question of when someone last installed. web-agent measured all twelve of admin's packages as already resolving to exactly what web pins — zero of twelve differed — so pinning changed no resolved version, and `npm ci --dry-run` exited 0 afterwards, which it cannot do unless package.json and the lockfile agree. `packages/contracts`, `packages/sdk` and `packages/testing` are DELIBERATELY NOT MEMBERS: they are not npm packages, and adding them changes what `npm install` does to trees that do not want it.
//workspaces CORRECTED 2026-09-09 — `pac: The sentence above gave a REASON rather than a rule, and the reason does not hold for this member, so it is superseded rather than ignored. It was written before any generated output existed. THE DEFECT IT WAS CONCEALING: 0037 requires generated types to be CONSUMED and never re-declared, and NO CONSUMER COULD IMPORT ONE — `packages/contracts` was not a member and neither client carried an alias, so the generator's entire output was unreachable from the two trees it was built for. web-agent found this while blocked on the Milestone 1 type swap, established it could add a tsconfig path and a Vite alias inside its OWN boundary, and argued against doing so: a per-client resolution of a shared thing is the divergence 0040 exists to end, and `architecture.md` §1 calls a shape one client has and the other does not a CONTRACT defect rather than a client-local workaround. THAT REFUSAL IS WHY THE FIX IS AT THE ROOT. The stated cost — 'changes what `npm install` does to trees that do not want it' — is ZERO here and was measured, not assumed: the package declares no dependencies and no peerDependencies because the 17 generated modules export TYPES ONLY, so `npm install` registers a symlink and resolves nothing. `packages/sdk` and `packages/testing` remain non-members and the original reason still holds for them. THE `exports` MAP IS THE POINT: it resolves `@dudo/contracts/<path>` to `./generated/<path>.ts` and exposes NOTHING else, so a client cannot import the generator, the schemas, the YAML or the validators — module resolution refuses. `clients consume contracts and never execute them` stops being a README sentence and becomes a build failure.

scripts.//typecheck: Both trees. `packages/testing` was checked by NOTHING until 2026-09-05, which concealed a fixture that had silently stopped composing what production composes while 400+ assertions kept passing — the suites reported on a shape the product no longer had. The gate landed red with 14 diagnostics and was deliberately kept OUT of this script until it was green, because a red gate folded into a green one makes the green one worthless. It is green as of 2026-09-05 and is now part of the gate. Three of the original 14 were exactly the drift it was added to catch.
scripts.typecheck: npm run typecheck:core && npm run typecheck:tests
scripts.//check:contracts: RETIRED 2026-09-05, the same day it was added, and deliberately not by deleting a check. Unsatisfiable request shapes — a `required` field absent from `properties` under `additionalProperties: false` — are now asserted by `packages/testing/suites/contracts/satisfiability.ts`, which is `qa-agent`'s and is strictly richer: same walk, plus a proof that the walker descends into nested `properties`/`items`/`allOf`, plus a mirror control proving it does not flag everything. `architecture.md` §1 assigns the shape — *producer and consumer are both tested against the contract by `qa-agent`* — and this was a test wearing root tooling's clothes. Retired by this repository's own rule for duplicate checks: two checks are both worth keeping only when each would go red on an input the other passes, and this one would not. It found four real defects first, including `login-v1`'s, which is why the suite case exists at all.
scripts.//test: The four suite entry points. Added 2026-09-05 after `qa-agent` pointed out that NOTHING invoked `packages/testing/**` — `typecheck:tests` only TYPE-checks it. So the suites, the six negative controls, the type-negative probe, every registry-coherence check and the contract-satisfiability case were reachable only by an agent typing their paths, and the contract check had just been moved OUT of `typecheck` on the argument that a suite case runs more often than root tooling. That argument was backwards and this script is what makes it true. All four set a non-zero exit code on failure, so it gates correctly. `run-az2-timing.ts` is DELIBERATELY ABSENT and is not an oversight: it is a measurement rather than a test, and its own header records why — a wall-clock threshold on a shared laptop fails for reasons unrelated to the code, and a suite that goes red under load teaches a team to ignore red. The structural proof of equal work lives in `suites/az2-login/equal-work.ts` and holds on any machine.
scripts.//test GATE COMPOSITION, 2026-09-09: `check:source-bytes` IS NOW PART OF THE GATE — the condition this file set for itself (`each goes into the gate the day it exits 0, and neither before`) was met, and met by the mechanism the user chose rather than by removing the bytes. It runs FIRST because it is cheap and a control-byte regression should fail before 500+ suite cases do. IT EXITS 0 BY QUARANTINE, NOT BY CLEANLINESS: one file carries three pinned NULs at exact byte offsets, and the pin FAILS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS — more is a regression, fewer means someone fixed it and must lower the pin in that change, because a pin left claiming a defect that no longer exists is a PESSIMISTIC STALE NUMBER, the kind §11a records is never questioned. VERIFIED RATHER THAN OBSERVED: four mutants run against the real tree — pin too low, pin too high, same count at different offsets, quarantined file gone — ALL FOUR EXIT 1, with the unmutated script exiting 0 as the floor. `check:route-fields` STAYS OUT, still red on 0034 phase 3, and joins on the same terms the day it exits 0.
scripts.//check:route-fields JOINED THE GATE 202: It exited 0 the moment BOTH halves of 0034 phase 3 landed — the contract's deprecated `identifier` alias removed by architecture-agent, the route's declared field removed by core-agent — plus 0039's `.session` drop. Measured before folding it in, not inferred: `target_identifier` present on both sides, zero bare `identifier` keys left in the contract, zero `identity.session.organization*` ids left in Core, and the checker reporting `15 routes, 10 contract operations, 6 matched, 6 with a comparable request shape (self-test passed)`. THE CHECK ITSELF IS THE PROOF THE TWO HALVES AGREE: it compares them in both directions and goes red if they are split across commits, which is why it read red for the half hour between the two landings. That red was the check working. BOTH CHECKS ARE NOW IN THE GATE, which is what Milestone 0 item 3 asked for (docs/decisions/0035). Ordering: the two cheap structural checks run first so a regression fails before 500+ suite cases do.
scripts.test: npm run check:schema-parse && npm run check:source-bytes && npm run check:route-fields && npm run check:request-class && npm run check:row-writes && node tools/run-suites.mjs
scripts.//check:schema-parse: EVERY JSON FILE UNDER packages/contracts/** PARSES — NOT ONLY THE ONES SOMETHING IMPORTS. It runs FIRST because a malformed schema makes every later check report consequences instead of causes. THE DEFECT IT EXISTS FOR HAPPENED 2026-09-10 AND WAS CAUGHT BY LUCK OF REFERENCE: two `$comment` blocks were appended to template-v1.schema.json without the comma a property value requires, and it surfaced as SIX generator refusals — one GEN_SCHEMA_UNREADABLE and five GEN_UNRESOLVABLE_REF, because template-lifecycle-v1 resolves five URNs into the file that would not parse. It surfaced ONLY because something referenced it. buildSchemaIndex reports an unparseable schema when the emitter OPENS it, and the emitter opens what an admitted contract imports — so a malformed schema nothing references yet is invisible to the whole toolchain. SIX of the twenty-two files have no contract beside them (measured, printed every run), including both App/capability registries, and BOTH WERE EDITED THAT DAY. WHY IT IS ROOT TOOLING RATHER THAN A DISCIPLINE: architecture-agent owns packages/contracts/** and HAS NO BASH TOOL — Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep — so it cannot parse a file, ever. The Team Lead told it to 'parse the file after editing' and it correctly refused the advice as workflow.md §11a's refusal that names a remedy the tool does not accept. It adopted the shape-driven Grep it CAN run (a line ending in a bare quote followed by a line beginning with one) unconditionally after any schema edit, and named that sweep's own limit: it catches this defect class and would miss an unbalanced brace. This check is the parser it cannot run, sited with the party that can execute the remedy. VERIFIED RATHER THAN OBSERVED: a self-test drives a missing comma and its mirror before anything real is read; a floor of 20 files fails a walk that examines nothing, because an empty glob reports zero unparseable files and reads exactly like success; and a mutant planted a missing colon in capability-manifest.schema.json — a file NO CONTRACT REFERENCES — giving exit 1, '22 examined, 1 unparseable', naming the file, against a control of exit 0. It says the files are well-formed JSON and NOTHING about whether they are valid JSON Schema; nothing in this repository executes JSON Schema.
scripts.//check:request-class: THE ENFORCEMENT 0039 CLAIMED AND DID NOT HAVE. The ADR said a declared `requestClass:` would be checked against the route tables; NOTHING CHECKED IT, and that was proved by construction rather than suspected. The generator cannot do it — a tool in packages/contracts/** parsing platform/core/** would make the contract set depend on Core's FILE LAYOUT, so Core could not refactor its own route tables without breaking a contracts-side tool. A cross-boundary comparison belongs at the boundary, which is scripts/ and the Team Lead's. It IMPORTS the four registries rather than parsing them — preAuthEntryPoints(), sessionRoutes(), platformRoutes() and createCoreRouter().routes — because a regex over route tables is a second implementation of Core's registration that disagrees with the first one silently, and the two Action routes prove it: their ids are literals INSIDE FACTORY FUNCTIONS, so a check looking for exported arrays finds three tables of four and reports a clean sweep of a corpus it never enumerated. THE POPULATION IS DERIVED TWICE BY MECHANISMS THAT SHARE NOTHING — the five executed registries (knows types, not files) against a textual sweep of every dotted id literal under platform/core AND apps (knows files, not types) — and a disagreement in EITHER direction fails, because a route table this file has never heard of would otherwise render as a clean run. *** THE FIRST VERSION ENUMERATED FOUR REGISTRIES AND SWEPT ONLY platform/core, SO BOTH DERIVATIONS AGREED WHILE MISSING THE CUSTOMERS APP'S TEN ROUTE IDS — 24 reported against a real 34. TWO DERIVATIONS THAT SHARE A SCOPE ARE ONE DERIVATION: they disagree about method and agree about blindness, and the blindness is the whole thing a population check is for. 0039 names two Action tables and the first version enumerated one. *** A SIXTH APP IS NOT SILENTLY MISSED: its ids appear in the textual sweep with no registry holding them and the run goes RED naming them — the registry list is a snapshot, being told the snapshot is stale is not. VERIFIED RATHER THAN OBSERVED: six mutants against a scratch COPY of the tree (packages/contracts/** is architecture-agent's and was not touched) — a class contradicting the registry two ways, a per-operation declaration overriding the contract level, a stray id in Core, a stray id in an APP, an unknown class name — ALL SIX EXIT 1, control 0. AND A FLOOR ON THE READER, ADDED AFTER IT WAS EARNED: a one-character extractor bug (storing the regex match rather than its capture group) made an early run exit 0 announcing '10 declared route ids agree' and '0 still undeclared', with all three self-tests passing, because they drove the pure comparison functions and the defect was in what the check could SEE. Joined the gate the day it exited 0, on the same terms as the two checks before it. 0.1s.
scripts.//check:row-writes: A PLATFORM ROUTE'S DECLARED maxRowWrites MUST BE AT LEAST WHAT THE DISPATCHER CHARGES. PLATFORM_OPERATOR_ACTION_ROW_WRITES was 2 when the platform contracts were written; 0016_platform_operator_action_indexes.sql moved it to 4 — its own comment saying the constant 'is moved in identity/control-plane-admission.ts in the same change'. The constant moved, NINE contract figures did not, and nothing compared them, so nothing went red. workflow.md §12's value-change limit exactly: a symbol that MOVES is caught by the compiler, a symbol whose VALUE moves is caught by nobody. It was found by security-agent deriving a free-tier exhaustion threshold from a contract's declared 2 and reporting figures wrong by a factor of two — in the PESSIMISTIC direction, the one §11a records that nobody catches. THE TWO-OFF IS WHAT DISGUISED IT: a route declaring 3 against a reservation of 4 reads as a rounding difference rather than a stale constant, so the write routes looked consistent and usage's 2 looked like the outlier; every one was understated by the same 2. IT IS A LOWER BOUND AND SAYS SO: every platform route writes the P4 audit record, so a figure below the charge is impossible rather than optimistic — but maxRowWrites is the route's own writes PLUS that record, and nothing here knows a handler's own write count, so a figure at or above the charge is not thereby correct. THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THE DECLARED REQUEST CLASS, NEVER THE FILE PATH: audit-read-v1 and business-read-v1 declare 0 legitimately (tenant Actions, P4 does not apply) and organization-selection-v1 declares 3 (session class), and a path-keyed check would have swept the session contract while covering the unclassified platform routes by accident — green, wrong, and unfalsifiable. UNCLASSIFIED ROUTES ARE PRINTED, NOT SKIPPED, and that reporting produced the finding nobody predicted: 27 of 43 operations carry no requestClass:, so 0039 PHASE 1's BACKLOG IS NOW BOUNDING A SECOND CHECK — twenty-four routes owing that field stopped being documentation debt the moment a check keyed on it existed, and check:request-class's own output cannot say so because it reports the backlog as what the sweep owes rather than as what other checks cannot see. RUN AGAINST THE REAL BROKEN STATE FIRST (§11a): exit 1 naming platform.organizations.list and platform.session.whoami declaring 0 — not stale-by-2 but never-right, a claim that P4 does not apply made by the contract that establishes P4, one line above its own 'audit: required'. Had it been built after the sweep it would have been green over nine routes and read as green over the class. VERIFIED RATHER THAN OBSERVED: a self-test drives five constructed operations before anything real is read, with the floor ON THE READER rather than only on the result — because if the maxRowWrites pattern stops matching, every route lands in 'missing', which this script reports and does not fail on, so a broken reader would print OK over a corpus it never read. A mutant breaking that pattern on a scratch copy exits 2 naming the three unread figures, against a control of 0. It reads the constant from Core rather than holding a copy, and reuses parseContract rather than adding a second contract parser — a second reader of one file being the defect this check exists for, one layer up. Joined the gate the day it exited 0, on the same terms as the three checks before it.
scripts.//check:source-bytes CORRECTED 2026-09-0: TWO CLAIMS BELOW ARE OVERSTATED AND BOTH WERE MEASURED, WITH NEGATIVE CONTROLS. (1) `git diff` renders a NUL-bearing file as binary ONLY WHEN THE NUL IS NEAR THE TOP: git samples just the first block for its binary test. platform/core's two files carry their NULs at bytes 34,135 and 40,922 and KEPT NORMAL TEXTUAL DIFFS THROUGHOUT — `--numstat` gave 8/1 and 12/3 with a NUL still present. A scratch-repo probe confirmed it independently: NUL at byte 10 diffs binary, at 34,135 and 40,922 textual, control without a NUL textual. SO THE SENTENCE BELOW ABOUT THE REVIEW TOOL BEING DISABLED WAS NEVER TRUE OF THESE FILES, and it was the argument that made the remediation urgent. The GREPPABILITY harm is real and unchanged; the REVIEWABILITY harm was not happening. (2) `plain grep found NOTHING` is true of THIS SHELL'S grep — a ugrep wrapper passing -I — and false of /usr/bin/grep, which reads these files correctly; `grep -a` works. BOTH were real observations generalised one step too far. The original text is kept below unedited because it is what the team believed and acted on.
scripts.//check:source-bytes: Scans every source file for control bytes. WHY IT EXISTS: three NUL bytes in `platform-route-handlers.ts` made `file` report it as `data`, so plain `grep` found NOTHING in a 1,652-line file — no match, no error, not even a zero from `grep -c ''`. It produced a false negative that nearly sent core-agent to build a handler already at line 1202, and it had been silently degrading every search of that file for days, including any security sweep that used plain grep. WORSE, AND THE REASON THIS IS ROOT TOOLING RATHER THAN A LINT PREFERENCE: `git diff` reports such a file as `Bin 11422 -> 13052 bytes, 0 insertions, 0 deletions`. THE REVIEW TOOL IS DISABLED BY THE DEFECT, so everything committed to those files landed unreviewable. On its first run it found ELEVEN bytes in SIX files across FOUR owners — not the three in one that were reported — including `pagination/cursor.ts` and `identity/pre-auth-admission.ts`, which nobody knew about and which sit on the pagination and login paths. Every one is correct in MEANING and wrong in FORM: deliberate domain separators and deliberate test inputs, typed as raw bytes instead of `String.fromCharCode(0)`. It ships with a known-failing input built at run time and refuses to report at all if that self-test does not fire — constructed rather than committed because `Write` cannot emit a NUL and the shell is what workflow.md §9 forbids.
scripts.//check:route-fields: Compares each platform route's declared `fields ∪ objectFields` against its contract's request `properties`, in BOTH directions. WHY: `platform.organizations.create` advertised `display_name` in its contract and did not declare it on the route, and the class refuses undeclared fields BEFORE authentication — so the first client to trust the contract would have failed EVERY onboarding, on the route that creates customers. web-agent found that one by reading, wired the field, and did not send it. This check is what finds the next one, and it found a second on its first run. It reads the three injected confirmation field names from their owning module rather than hardcoding them, so it does not go stale when that mechanism is renamed, and refuses to run if it cannot read them. Population reported against an independently derived expectation rather than as a bare count: 6 of 7 body-carrying routes are comparable, and the seventh states its request in prose because its body is only the injected fields.
scripts.//COUNT CORRECTED 2026-09-09: The entry below said `five files still carry control bytes`. MEASURED TODAY: TWO. `platform/core/platform/platform-route-handlers.ts` (2 NULs, lines 936 and 957) and `platform/web/scripts/verify-kdf.mjs` (1 DEL). `pre-auth-admission.ts` is CLEAN — plain grep over it went from 0 matches to 66. THIS IS NOT BOOKKEEPING: architecture-agent cited the stale five to scope how far it trusted its own negative searches, so a wrong count in this file was bounding another agent's confidence about a different tree. A COUNT IN A COMMENT IS AN ASSERTION THAT ROTS, and this one rotted downward, which is the direction that makes the world look worse than it is and nobody double-checks. The authority is `npm run check:source-bytes`, which prints the population and the files; prefer running it to reading this.
scripts.//SUPERSEDED 2026-09-09 — ONE OF THE TWO: The entry below is kept because it records the RULE, which held and was followed: a red gate folded into a green one makes the green one worthless, so each check waited until it exited 0. `check:source-bytes` reached 0 on 2026-09-09 and joined `test` the same day. `check:route-fields` has NOT, and stays out. Read the entry below as the standing policy for the second check, not as a description of the first.
scripts.//WHY THESE TWO ARE NOT IN A GATE YET: BOTH EXIT 1 TODAY, ON REAL FINDINGS — five files still carry control bytes, and `platform.organizations.members.resolve` declares `identifier` while its contract publishes `target_identifier`. They are deliberately NOT chained into `test` or `typecheck`, for the reason recorded in `//typecheck` above and applied there first: A RED GATE FOLDED INTO A GREEN ONE MAKES THE GREEN ONE WORTHLESS. The precedent is `typecheck:tests`, which landed red with 14 diagnostics, was held out until it was green, and only then became part of the gate. THE CONDITION FOR FOLDING THESE IN IS THE SAME AND IS NOT A JUDGEMENT CALL: each goes into the gate the day it exits 0, and neither before. Until then they are run by name, and their findings are tracked as defects rather than tolerated as noise — which is the failure mode of a permanently-red check nobody folds in.
scripts.//migrations: LOCAL variants act on the local simulated D1 and are safe to run freely. REMOTE variants act on the deployed database and are a production-class action requiring explicit user approval each time (.claude/rules/security.md §7). They are separate scripts, and named, so neither can be run by accident.
scripts.//deploy: There is no `deploy` script, deliberately. Deployment is gated on C5 and on explicit user approval; a one-word npm script is exactly the wrong affordance for an action that needs a decision.
scripts.//deploy:staging REMOVED 2026-09-08: It read `wrangler deploy --env staging` and POINTED AT A TARGET THAT DOES NOT EXIST: neither wrangler.jsonc nor wrangler.admin.jsonc defines an `env` at all. Nobody had run it, so nobody had found out. WORSE THAN A BROKEN SCRIPT, IT WAS A FALSE ASSURANCE — its presence implied a staging environment existed, and every deploy so far went straight to the real app/api/admin.dudo.work hostnames while a script sat here suggesting otherwise. THE USER RULED ON 2026-09-08 (docs/decisions/0035) that dudo.work IS the test environment, named honestly, and that this script goes. Deployment stays a deliberate wrangler invocation requiring explicit user approval every time (.claude/rules/security.md §7). REOPEN THIS BEFORE THE FIRST REAL CUSTOMER — that event, not a date, is what makes `dudo.work is the test environment` false, and it will not announce itself.
